outputs.L1:
Here is an eloquent, professional modern prose adaptation that faithfully preserves all the original meaning, imagery, and emotional depth:

***

"Where we are no longer matters, and I ask that no one speak to me of comfort. Let us speak instead of graves, of worms, and of epitaphs. Let the dust be our paper, and with our tears, let us write our sorrow upon the bosom of the earth. Let us appoint executors and discuss our wills—and yet, what is there left to bequeath, save our dethroned bodies to the ground? Our lands, our lives, and all that we possessed now belong to Bolingbroke. We can call nothing our own except death, and that small mound of barren earth which acts as a shroud over our bones.

For heaven’s sake, let us sit upon the ground and tell tragic stories of the deaths of kings: how some were overthrown, some slain in battle, some haunted by the ghosts of those they deposed, some poisoned by their wives, and others murdered in their sleep—all meeting a violent end. For within the hollow crown that encircles a king’s mortal head, Death holds his court. There sits the jester, mocking the monarch's grandeur and grinning at his pomp, allowing him a brief moment to rule, to be feared, and to command with a look—filling him with vanity as if his human flesh were impenetrable brass. Yet once Death has indulged him, he comes at last and, with a mere pin, pierces through his castle wall—and farewell, king!

Cover your heads, and do not mock frail human flesh with empty reverence. Cast aside respect, tradition, protocol, and formal duty, for you have misunderstood me all this time. I sustain myself on bread just as you do; I experience want, taste grief, and need friends. Subjected to these same human vulnerabilities, how can you possibly say to me that I am a king?"
outputs.L2:
It matters little where we are, so no one should try to offer me consolation. Instead, let our conversation center entirely on tombs, decay, and gravestone inscriptions. We ought to weep until our tears soak the dry dirt, recording our anguish upon the soil. We could discuss drafting wills and naming representatives to handle our estates, but that would be futile—for what remains for us to pass down to anyone, except for our defeated bodies returned to the dirt? Bolingbroke has seized our lands, our existence, and everything else we owned. Nothing truly belongs to us anymore except our own mortality and the tiny plot of barren ground that serves to cover our remains. 

I beg you, let us sit right here on the dirt and recount tragic tales about the violent demises of monarchs throughout history. Some were stripped of their power, others fell in battle, several were haunted by the spirits of the rulers they had dethroned, a few were poisoned by their own wives, and others were slain while sleeping; ultimately, every one of them was murdered. This occurs because Death holds court right inside the hollow ring of a king’s crown. There, Death sits like a mocking jester, ridiculing the ruler’s grandeur and laughing at his displays of power. Death allows the monarch a fleeting moment—a brief theatrical scene—to act sovereign, inspire terror, and slay with a glance, filling him with hollow arrogance until he believes his physical body is an impenetrable fortress of brass. Yet, after indulging the ruler’s vanity for a short while, Death simply pierces that castle wall with something as insignificant as a pin, and just like that, the king is gone!

So put your hats back on and stop offering solemn reverence to a creature of mere flesh and blood. Abandon all formal deference, ancient customs, courtly etiquette, and ritualistic duty. You have misjudged my true nature this entire time: I rely on ordinary food to survive, experience hardship, feel sorrow, and require friendship. Being subject to these universal human vulnerabilities, how can you possibly call me a king?
outputs.L3:
**The Hollow Crown: King Richard’s Confrontation with Mortality**

When faced with the catastrophic reality of his military and political defeat, King Richard undergoes a profound transformation, abandoning all hope of retaining his throne. Rather than accepting the comforting words or strategic advice of his remaining loyalists, Richard adamantly rejects all solace. He chooses instead to immerse himself fully in grief, fixating exclusively on thoughts of death, decay, and the absolute fragility of human existence. 

This deep despair stems from a sobering reality: Henry Bolingbroke has successfully seized control of both Richard's land and his life. In this moment of total dispossession, Richard comes to understand the fundamental illusion of earthly authority. He realizes that human beings possess no true, permanent ownership over kingdoms, wealth, or titles. When all worldly grandiosity is stripped away, the only property a person genuinely retains is the small plot of earth that will eventually house their mortal remains.

To make sense of his personal ruin, Richard broadens his view, contextualizing his fate within the violent history of the monarchy itself. He reflects on how rulers throughout time, despite their supreme authority, have consistently met tragic and treacherous ends. Whether deposed, poisoned, slain in battle, or betrayed by their closest advisers, kings are exposed to a unique and dangerous vulnerability. Far from offering true protection, the throne serves only to make its occupant a target for ambition and violence.

This tragic irony of royal power is vivid through the personification of Death. Richard imagines Death not as a distant force, but as a mocking court jester residing within the hollow center of the royal crown itself. There, Death sits, allowing the monarch a brief, fleeting period to play at being a god—granting him a false sense of absolute power and invincibility. Yet, this divine majesty is merely a cruel joke. At any moment, with something as simple as a pinprick, Death easily pierces the king’s fragile defense, destroying him in an instant and exposing the utter vanity of his rule.

Having unmasked the illusion of royal supremacy, Richard completely abandons the traditional ceremonies, flatteries, and reverent behaviors expected at court. He urges his companions to discard the solemn respect typically paid to an anointed sovereign, asking them instead to view him as an ordinary man. Stripped of the divine right of kings, Richard openly acknowledges that he is subject to the exact same physical needs, emotional griefs, and physical weaknesses as any common subject. Ultimately, in accepting his impending demise, Richard dismantles the myth of royalty, revealing that beneath the crown, every king is simply human.
outputs.L4:
The castle walls no longer stand as a fortress of safety, but as a monument to an impending end. Surrounded by the rising tide of rebellion and stripped of his military advantage, King Richard II experiences a profound existential rupture. The divine right of kings—a doctrine that had fortified his identity and absolute authority for a lifetime—shatters under the weight of cold, political reality. Faced with the imminent loss of his crown, Richard does not reach for weapons or rally his remaining men with hollow promises of victory. Instead, he turns inward, discarding the grand theater of statecraft to address the fundamental futility of earthly power.

In a dramatic departure from regal decorum, Richard actively rejects the comforting illusions of royal ceremony. He casts aside the expectation of kingly defiance and invites his remaining courtiers to abandon their deference and sit upon the bare ground—a symbolic act of profound humility and reduction. Dismissing empty flatteries, he calls for a turn toward absolute realism: "Let’s talk of graves, of worms, and epitaphs." 

Free from the distraction of his former glory, Richard casts his gaze backward into history, evoking a haunting chronicle of past monarchs whose sacred blood could not shield them from violence. He reflects upon the tragic fates of those who came before him: kings who were deposed, slain in war, haunted by the ghosts of those they ousted, poisoned by their wives, or murdered in their sleep. In Richard’s tragic vision, the chronicle of royalty is not a triumph of legacy, but a grim procession of dead sovereigns, all reduced to dusty memories despite their once-absolute power.

At the heart of Richard’s meditation is a striking, morbid image: Death depicted as a mocking jester—an "antic"—that sits within the hollow circumference of the mortal king's crown. This sinister figure allows the monarch a brief, fleeting scene to play the sovereign: to act grandly, to inflict fear, and to self-delude into believing his body is made of impregnable brass. Yet this sovereign glory is merely a cruel joke. At his leisure, the jester comes with a simple, quiet gesture—a tiny pin—and pierces through the castle walls of the king's self-deception, shattering the grand armor of royalty in an instant.

Through this agonizing epiphany, the rigid boundary between the sovereign and the subject completely dissolves. Death’s inevitable triumph exposes the illusion of royal invincibility, revealing that beneath the anointed oil and ermine robes, kings are bound by the same physical and emotional frailties as the lowest of their subjects. Richard demands that his followers stop treating him as an untouchable deity, famously acknowledging his own raw, vulnerable humanity: he lives by bread, feels want, tastes grief, and requires friends. Ultimately, as Richard watches his kingdom slip away, his surrender of political authority yields a darker, universal truth: that earthly power is a fleeting shadow, and in the shadow of mortality, all human beings are rendered equal.
outputs.L5:
The shadow of the crown hung heavy in the quiet stone hall. For years, the realm had known him only by his grand titles, but in the solitary midnight hours, he was stripped of pretense. He was simply Richard—a man sculpted by duty, burdened by the terrible weight of his own lineage. 

Outside the high arched windows, a summer storm battered the fortress, echoing the unrest that brewed at the borders of his domain. To the world, he was a sovereign of iron will, the grand King whose name was etched into decrees and spoken in hushed tones of reverence and fear. Yet, beneath the velvet mantle, Richard felt the fragile, mortal rhythm of his own heart. He knew that kingdoms were fragile things, built on the shifting sands of loyalty and ambition.

He stepped toward the grand oak doors of the council chamber, where his generals awaited his final command. The time for hesitation had passed. 

He turned to his closest advisor, a weary smile breaking through his stern countenance. "Open the gates," Richard commanded, his voice steady despite the tempest raging outside. "**Let** the storm come, and **let** history judge what we do tonight. If fate demands our stand, then **let** us face it not as men who fear the dark, but as those who carry the light."

With a nod, the heavy doors were pushed open, and King Richard stepped forward into the dawn of his destiny.

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me the text of King Richard's monologue from Act 3, Scene 2 of Shakespeare's Richard II, where he despairs over Bolingbroke's rise. Make sure to note the character and play at the beginning.
counterfactuals.output:
**Play:** *Richard II* by William Shakespeare  
**Character:** King Richard II  
**Act 3, Scene 2**

***

**KING RICHARD II:**

No matter where; of comfort no man speak:
Let’s talk of graves, of worms, and epitaphs;
Make dust our paper and with rainy eyes
Write sorrow on the bosom of the earth,
Let’s choose executors and talk of wills:
And yet not so, for what can we bequeath
Save our deposed bodies to the ground?
Our lands, our lives and all are Bolingbroke’s,
And nothing can we call our own but death
And that small model of the barren earth
Which serves as paste and cover to our bones.
For God’s sake, let us sit upon the ground
And tell sad stories of the death of kings:
How some have been deposed; some slain in war;
Some haunted by the ghosts they have deposed;
Some poison’d by their wives; some sleeping kill’d;
All murder’d: for within the hollow crown
That rounds the mortal temples of a king
Keeps Death his court and there the antic sits,
Scoffing his state and grinning at his pomp,
Allowing him a breath, a little scene,
To monarchize, be fear’d and kill with looks,
Infusing him with self and vain conceit,
As if this flesh which walls about our life
Were brass impregnable, and humour’d thus
Comes at the last and with a little pin
Bores through his castle wall, and farewell king!
Cover your heads and mock not flesh and blood
With solemn reverence: throw away respect,
Tradition, form and ceremonious duty,
For you have but mistook me all this while:
I live with bread like you, feel want,
Taste grief, need friends: subjected thus,
How can you say to me, I am a king?
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

The speech you are looking for is King Richard’s famous monologue from William Shakespeare’s **_Richard II_ (Act 3, Scene 2)**.

Here is the monologue in full:

***

**KING RICHARD II:**

### Why this monologue stands out:
* **The Personification of Death:** Richard paints a vivid image of Death sitting inside the "hollow crown" like a court jester ("the antic"), mocking the king's temporary power before easily destroying him with a "little pin."
